section_summary: This section documents internal Japanese political developments from April 1936 to February 1937, centering on the cabinet instability following the February 26 Incident. It covers the formation, policies, and eventual collapse of the Hirota Cabinet amid intense Army pressure and parliamentary friction over foreign policy and state control. It further details the subsequent failure of General Kazushige Ugaki to form a government due to Army opposition, followed by the establishment and initial measures of the Hayashi Cabinet.

subfiles.about: Report on the formation of the Hirota Cabinet and its statement of policy following the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: Documents the resignation of the Okada Cabinet and the selection of Koki Hirota after Prince Konoe declined. It details the Army's four major demands, objections to proposed liberal ministers, and the eventual compromise cabinet composition. Deaths of Commerce Minister Kawasaki and former Foreign Minister Uchida are also reported.
subfiles.title: Formation of the Hirota Cabinet and its Statement of Policy

subfiles.about: Memorandum regarding newly promulgated ordinances requiring service ministers to be active duty officers.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes Tokyo reports of an imperial ordinance restricting appointments of War and Navy Ministers and Vice Ministers to active-list officers. Notes that while reserve officers were legally eligible under prior law, none were appointed in practice. Emphasizes that the political motive behind the amendment is evident.
subfiles.title: Amendment of Regulations Governing Appointment of War and Navy Ministers

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Imperial Ordinances Nos. 63 and 64 restricting military ministerial appointments to the active list.
subfiles.summary: Transmits official English translations of Imperial Ordinances Nos. 63 and 64 limiting Army and Navy Ministers and Vice Ministers to active generals and admirals. Explains that the military sought to formally revoke the 1913 regulation that allowed reserve officers to hold these portfolios. Countersigned by Prime Minister Hirota and service ministers Terauchi and Nagano.
subfiles.title: Revision of Regulations Governing Appointment of Army and Navy Ministers and Vice Ministers

subfiles.about: Despatch on Ambassador Saburo Kurusu's travels through the United States and his domestic political prospects.
subfiles.summary: Reports on the transit of newly appointed Ambassador to Belgium Saburo Kurusu through the United States to promote commercial understanding and address trade friction. Includes press translations highlighting efforts to resolve textile and trade quotas between the two nations. Relates Foreign Office confirmations that Kurusu was slated to assume a future cabinet portfolio upon returning from Brussels.
subfiles.title: Mission of Ambassador Saburo Kurusu and Cabinet Rumors

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on Imperial Ordinance No. 61 abolishing the Cabinet Inquiry Council.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet noting Embassy Despatch No. 1816 regarding Imperial Ordinance No. 61 promulgated on May 5, 1936. The ordinance provided for the formal abolition of the Naikaku Shingi Kai (Cabinet Inquiry Council). Filed originally under 894.00/649.
subfiles.title: Abolition of the Naikaku Shingi Kai (Cabinet Inquiry Council)

subfiles.about: Political report on developments during April 1936 affecting the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Details the abolition of the Cabinet Deliberative Body and the formal installation of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister. Outlines disciplinary reprimands issued against metropolitan police officials connected with the February 26 Incident. Highlights regular Friday coordination meetings instituted among the Foreign, War, and Navy Ministers to unify foreign policy and defense.
subfiles.title: Developments During the Month of April, 1936, Which Affected the Cabinet

subfiles.about: Political review of cabinet affairs and political reform discussions during June 1936.
subfiles.summary: Observes the lack of definitive administrative and social reform by the Hirota Cabinet despite continuing Army pressure. Discusses proposals for Diet reform commissions and the rejection of a system of ministers without portfolio. Summarizes speeches at the prefectural governors conference reflecting official apprehension regarding subversive undercurrents.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs: The Cabinet (June 1936)

subfiles.about: Summary of cabinet deliberations on national policy priorities and ministerial friction in July 1936.
subfiles.summary: Enumerates the six major policy programs selected for cabinet consideration, including defense increases, tax readjustment, and electric power nationalization. Explains that collective cabinet deliberation was abandoned due to internal friction and military insistence on budgetary priority. Concludes that defense ministries are progressively asserting control over government policy.
subfiles.title: The Hirota Cabinet: Developments of July, 1936

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on the arrest and trial of former Railways Minister Shinya Uchida for bribery.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 2128 reporting on the arrest and trial of Shinya Uchida, former Minister of Railways in the Okada Cabinet. Uchida was charged with receiving bribes during his ministerial tenure. Originally classified under 894.00/673.
subfiles.title: Arrest and Trial of Shinya Uchida

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting growing sentiment favoring the resignation of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Reports mounting nationwide sentiment demanding the resignation of the Hirota Cabinet in the wake of the Anti-Comintern Pact with Germany. Assesses that while public attacks cite the German agreement, the true underlying cause of dissatisfaction is diplomatic failure in China. Analyzes whether a cabinet resignation would alleviate international concerns regarding Japan's foreign policy orientation.
subfiles.title: Sentiment Favoring the Resignation of the Hirota Cabinet

subfiles.about: Monthly political review covering cabinet activities and administrative reform plans in October 1936.
subfiles.summary: Reports on stalled administrative reform proposals and intense public opposition to Army suggestions that Diet members be barred from cabinet posts. Outlines the compromise plan approved in principle for state control of the electric power industry based on private ownership and public operation. Notes the plan faced anticipated resistance from commercial interests and the Diet.
subfiles.title: Japanese Cabinet: Activities and Administrative Reform (October 1936)

subfiles.about: Account of joint Army-Navy recommendations for administrative reform and parliamentary friction in November 1936.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes a joint reform proposal submitted by the Vice Ministers of War and Navy advocating government reorganization, departmental amalgamations, and Diet revision. Details the War Minister's public denial of intent to reduce Diet powers following widespread popular backlash against military interference. Notes joint opposition by the Big Five private electric utilities against proposed power nationalization.
subfiles.title: Administrative Reform Recommendations and Diet Controversy

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on a Chinese newspaper editorial analyzing the Japanese cabinet crisis.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 264 from Nanking summarizing an editorial from the Nanking Hsin Ching Jih Pao published on October 13, 1936. The editorial analyzed the potential adverse international and bilateral consequences of a Japanese cabinet collapse. Originally filed under 894.00/674.
subfiles.title: Editorial on Japanese Cabinet Crisis (Nanking Hsin Ching Jih Pao)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on the diplomatic difficulties and domestic position of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 2187 reporting on the vulnerable domestic position of the Japanese cabinet. It emphasizes the escalating difficulties experienced by the ministry in connection with foreign policy and negotiations with China. Originally filed under 793.94/8485.
subfiles.title: Present Position of the Cabinet in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on the precarious status of the Hirota Cabinet resulting from foreign policy setbacks.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet referencing Despatch No. 2205 regarding the deteriorating position of the Hirota Cabinet at the close of 1936. Notes that the primary challenges threatening the government stemmed from diplomatic failures. Originally filed under 793.94/8500.
subfiles.title: Present Position of the Hirota Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting acute Diet opposition, the Hamada-Terauchi clash, and the two-day prorogation of parliament.
subfiles.summary: Describes the political showdown in the Diet sparked by a fierce verbal confrontation between Kunimatsu Hamada and War Minister Terauchi, resulting in a two-day prorogation. Details the Army's demand for parliamentary dissolution and its aggressive midnight manifesto insisting on nationalistic reform. Evaluates the cabinet's dissolution threat as coercive maneuvering against defiant political parties.
subfiles.title: Opposition to the Cabinet Displayed in the Diet and Prorogation

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that Diet dissolution and cabinet resignation appear inevitable.
subfiles.summary: Reports prevailing opinions among Japanese political leaders that the dissolution of the Diet and the subsequent fall of the Hirota Cabinet cannot be avoided. Cautions that major political crises in Japan have historically been resolved through unexpected compromises. Indicates that clarity is expected within the coming day.
subfiles.title: Impending Dissolution of the Diet and Resignation of the Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the submission of the Hirota Cabinet's collective resignation to the Emperor.
subfiles.summary: Confirms that Prime Minister Hirota tendered the collective resignation of his cabinet to the Emperor on the afternoon of January 23, 1937. Explains that the collapse was caused by the War Minister's absolute refusal to compromise with the political parties. Notes that General Kazushige Ugaki is prominently discussed as Hirota's potential successor.
subfiles.title: Resignation of the Japanese Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram assessing General Ugaki's prospects of forming a new cabinet despite reported Army opposition.
subfiles.summary: Advises that reliable sources indicate General Ugaki has a strong chance of successfully forming a government notwithstanding vocal Army opposition. Discounts newspaper rumors suggesting the appointment of General Matsui as Foreign Minister and Toshio Shiratori as Vice Minister. Anticipates that negotiations will require several days before reaching a resolution.
subfiles.title: Prospects of General Ugaki Forming a Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on a State Department memorandum analyzing the Japanese parliamentary crisis.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum prepared by Eugene H. Dooman of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on January 23, 1937. The memorandum provided a detailed résumé of the conflict between the political parties and the Hirota Cabinet. Originally filed under 894.00/683.
subfiles.title: Conflict Between Political Parties and the Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Army refusal to nominate a War Minister for General Ugaki's cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Reports continued Army obstructionism against General Ugaki and press disclosures that military authorities refuse to designate a War Minister for his cabinet. Outlines three potential outcomes should Ugaki report failure: an imperial mandate compelling Army compliance, or imperial commands to Prince Konoe or General Minami. Indicates Ugaki will not report failure to the Throne before the following day.
subfiles.title: Army Obstruction of General Ugaki's Cabinet Formation

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Ugaki's conference with the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal and renewed efforts to form a cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Reports that General Ugaki conferred at length with Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Kurahei Yuasa and subsequently announced the continuation of his cabinet-making mandate. Indicates that the Imperial Court is displeased with military intransigence and desires reconsideration by the Army. Highlights intense political tension, reflecting the strongest resistance to military dictation seen in fifteen years.
subfiles.title: General Ugaki Continues Efforts with Imperial Court Support

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting General Ugaki's formal failure to form a cabinet and public protest against Army political interference.
subfiles.summary: Reports that General Ugaki formally surrendered his imperial mandate to form a cabinet at noon on January 29, 1937. Details public statements released by Ugaki and his lieutenant resigning their military commissions and sharply castigating Army interference in constitutional governance. Notes that while domestic authorities suppressed the statements, their full text was telephoned abroad to the New York Herald Tribune.
subfiles.title: Failure of General Ugaki and Protests Against Army Dictation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on a State Department memorandum reviewing the parliamentary crisis and Ugaki's designation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum dated January 25, 1937, authored by Eugene H. Dooman of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. The paper provided an updated estimate of the parliamentary breakdown and analyzed the designation of General Ugaki. Originally filed under 894.00/687.
subfiles.title: Parliamentary Crisis and Designation of General Ugaki

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the selection and character appraisal of General Senjuro Hayashi as Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: Reports that Baron Hiranuma declined the premiership, leading to the selection of retired General Senjuro Hayashi, who enjoys broad military backing. Characterizes Hayashi as a disciplined, moderate soldier expected to minimize friction between the Army and the civil government. Observes that while his selection marks a victory for the military, business and financial circles express misgivings regarding impending industrial controls.
subfiles.title: Selection of General Senjuro Hayashi as Prime Minister

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the formal installation and ministerial lineup of the Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Reports the installation of the Hayashi Cabinet, noting multiple concurrent portfolios held by ministers pending administrative reorganization. Highlights that the appointment of moderate banker Toyotaro Yuki as Finance Minister significantly reassured financial circles against reckless spending. Observes that foreign affairs remains temporarily under Hayashi while prospective ambassadorial appointments are evaluated.
subfiles.title: Installation of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram providing an in-depth analysis of the character, policies, and political vulnerabilities of the Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes the Hayashi Cabinet as an opportunistic, transitional regime designed to bridge a constitutional crisis without immediate confrontation between Fascism and liberalism. Assesses the ministers, noting the prominence of Yuki as an adherent of Takahashi's sound financial orthodoxy and the selection of moderate Nakamura over radical military figures. Concludes that despite lacking party support, the government may survive if parliament avoids precipitating dissolution.
subfiles.title: Analysis of the New Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the public announcement of the Hayashi Cabinet's general policy platform.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the Hayashi Cabinet announced its official policy platform, consisting of five core points centered on national defense, national polity, and industrial expansion. Notes that the statement is phrased in vague and nebulous generalities that offer little concrete legislative detail. Indicates that a comprehensive written despatch will follow by mail.
subfiles.title: Announcement of Hayashi Cabinet Policies

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on a State Department memorandum discussing the composition of the new Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum by Eugene H. Dooman of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs written on February 2, 1937. The document reviews the newly installed Hayashi ministry and comments on the backgrounds and political orientations of its members. Originally filed under 894.00/692.
subfiles.title: Cabinet Crisis: The New Hayashi Ministry

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the appointment of General Hajime Sugiyama as War Minister and changes at the Bank of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reports that General Kotaro Nakamura resigned as War Minister due to illness and was succeeded by General Hajime Sugiyama, thereby strengthening military influence in the cabinet. Details major leadership transitions at the Bank of Japan, where Seihin Ikeda replaced Eigo Fukai as Governor alongside Vice Governor Juichi Tsushima. Financial circles welcomed the new economic leadership as a practical triumvirate capable of maintaining monetary stability.
subfiles.title: Appointment of General Sugiyama and Bank of Japan Reorganization

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing Prime Minister Hayashi's address to the House of Peers regarding foreign relations and budget policy.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes General Hayashi's conciliatory parliamentary address outlining a reduced budget, proposed tax increases, and desire to avoid Diet dissolution. Analyzes his foreign policy statements, noting a milder tone toward China, firm overtures to the Soviet Union, and reaffirmation of the German anti-Comintern pact. Highlights the deliberate omission of contentious issues concerning the United States to signal stable bilateral relations.
subfiles.title: General Hayashi's Speech Before the House of Peers

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note concerning diplomatic reports that Ambassador Naotake Sato was offered the Foreign Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram from Chargé d'Affaires Ray Atherton in London dated February 26, 1937. It reports information from Shigeru Yoshida indicating that Ambassador Naotake Sato in Paris had been approached to assume the post of Foreign Minister. Originally classified under 701.9451/13.
subfiles.title: Offer of Foreign Affairs Portfolio to Ambassador Sato

subfiles.about: Political review covering mounting political and diplomatic attacks against the Hirota Cabinet in December 1936.
subfiles.summary: Reviews the intense domestic criticism confronting the Hirota Cabinet during December 1936 from political parties and the press. Outlines grievances concerning the collapse of Sino-Japanese negotiations, excessive secrecy in concluding the anti-Comintern pact with Germany, and unfavorable world reaction. Text breaks off midsentence while discussing Foreign Minister Arita's disclosures regarding the pact.
subfiles.title: The Hirota Cabinet: Criticism and Developments (December 1936)
